nameStory: The chuck-will's-widow gets its name from its distinctive nighttime call that sounds exactly like someone clearly saying "chuck-will's-widow" over and over. This repetitive three-syllable call echoes through southern forests on warm summer nights, making it one of the few birds whose name perfectly matches what you'll hear.
description: The chuck-will's-widow is a mysterious nocturnal bird that's part of the nightjar family, known for their secretive nighttime habits. These medium-sized birds have mottled brown and gray feathers that provide perfect camouflage against tree bark and fallen leaves during the day. They're built for nighttime insect hunting, with large eyes, wide mouths, and soft flight feathers that allow them to fly silently through the darkness. In New England, they're quite rare, representing the northern edge of their range.

idTips.label: Distinctive Call
idTips.description: Listen for the clear, repetitive "chuck-will's-widow" call echoing through the night - it's slower and more deliberate than a whip-poor-will's rapid chant

idTips.label: Cryptic Plumage
idTips.description: Mottled brown, gray, and buff feathers create an intricate bark-like pattern that makes roosting birds nearly invisible against tree trunks

idTips.label: Large Gaping Mouth
idTips.description: When threatened, they open their mouth impossibly wide, revealing a bright pink or orange interior that can startle predators

idTips.label: Ground-level Flight
idTips.description: Often seen flying low over roads and clearings at dusk, their flight appears moth-like and erratic as they chase insects

idTips.label: Horizontal Roosting
idTips.description: During the day, they rest lengthwise along tree branches rather than perched upright, their camouflage making them look like a bump on the bark

habitat: In New England, chuck-will's-widow prefer open woodlands near water sources, particularly around Cape Cod and occasionally other coastal areas. They favor mixed forests with clearings where they can hunt insects, often near swamps, pond edges, or other wetland areas. Look for them in areas with a combination of trees for roosting and open spaces for nighttime foraging.

seasonality.spring: Arrive in late spring and begin their territorial calling, which is most intense during May and early June breeding season.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for calling and breeding, with adults hunting insects throughout warm summer nights.
seasonality.fall: Calling decreases significantly as birds prepare for migration, becoming much quieter by late summer.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England, having migrated south to the Caribbean and Central America.

funFact: Chuck-will's-widow have been recorded swallowing prey as large as small hummingbirds and warblers whole - their enormous mouths can open wide enough to engulf birds nearly as big as themselves, though they typically stick to large moths and beetles.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Eastern Whip-poor-will, but chuck-will's-widow have a distinctly different call - remember that "chuck-will's-widow" has three clear syllables while "whip-poor-will" sounds more like rapid machine-gun fire. Chuck-will's-widow are also noticeably larger and bulkier.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being primarily southern birds, chuck-will's-widow have small isolated populations that have established themselves in a few New England locations, particularly Cape Cod, representing fascinating examples of range expansion. These northern populations are quite rare and represent exciting finds for local birders.
compareHints: Compared to their close relative the Eastern Whip-poor-will, chuck-will's-widow are significantly larger and bulkier with a slower, more measured call rhythm. While whip-poor-will rapidly repeat their name up to 100 times per minute, chuck-will's-widow call at a more leisurely pace with longer pauses between repetitions. Chuck-will's-widow also prefer slightly more open habitats compared to the dense forest preference of whip-poor-will.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern Whip-poor-will's closest relative in our region is the Chuck-will's-widow, but that species barely reaches southern New England and has a different call that sounds like "chuck-will's-WID-ow.
